semantics: Free prompt-card deck for the Dialogic Reading tool (portfolio plan 3.6). Cards implement the CROWD prompt taxonomy (Completion, Recall, Open-ended, Wh-, Distancing) inside the PEER loop (Prompt, Evaluate, Expand, Repeat). IP rule, grader-enforced: cards reference book types and generic scenes only; no card may name, quote, or paraphrase a specific published book. Type-correctness is grader-enforced: a Completion card must contain an ellipsis blank, a Recall card must ask about what happened, an Open-ended card must invite description, a Wh- card must open with a wh-word, and a Distancing card must bridge from the book to the child's own life. Age bands bound prompt length: younger bands get shorter prompts.

completion.label: Completion
completion.explainer: Leave a blank at the end of a familiar line and let your child fill it in. Pause longer than feels natural.

recall.label: Recall
recall.explainer: Ask about something that already happened in the book. Great for rereads, which is most reads.

open_ended.label: Open-ended
open_ended.explainer: Point at a busy page and hand over the microphone. There is no wrong answer; whatever they say, add one detail and keep going.

wh.label: Wh- questions
wh.explainer: What, where, who questions that build vocabulary. Point at the thing you're asking about.

distancing.label: Distancing
distancing.explainer: Bridge from the page to your child's own life. These are the hardest and the most valuable; they turn a book into a conversation about their world.

peer.body: Invite your child to say something about the page, using any card from this deck.
Respond warmly to what they actually said. Every attempt counts.
Say their answer back with one word added. 'Doggy' becomes 'Yes, a muddy doggy!'
Give them a chance to use the bigger version, without demanding it.

cards.prompt_text: The cow says...
cards.follow_up: Any sound counts. Echo it back with delight, then add the word: 'Moo! The cow says moo!'

cards.prompt_text: The baby is going to...
cards.follow_up: If they say 'sleep' or 'bed', expand it: 'Yes, going to sleep in her cozy bed.'

cards.prompt_text: The fire truck goes...
cards.follow_up: Sirens, vrooms, and 'wee-oo' all count as answers. Join in first, expand after.

cards.prompt_text: On a familiar page, stop before the last word: 'And then the bear fell...'
cards.follow_up: Rereads make this easy on purpose. The pause is the prompt; hold it a beat longer than comfortable.

cards.prompt_text: He ate the apple, and the pear, and the...
cards.follow_up: List pages are built for this. Let them finish the list, then count the foods together.

cards.prompt_text: Stop mid-rhyme and let them land the rhyming word: 'The frog sat on a...'
cards.follow_up: Rhyme completion is early phonological practice. If they land a silly non-rhyme, celebrate it and offer both.

cards.prompt_text: Goodnight lamp, goodnight chair, goodnight...
cards.follow_up: Let them run the goodnight list right off the page and into the actual room. That jump is the win.

cards.prompt_text: Start the page's sentence and trail off: 'And the dog is...'
cards.follow_up: In a wordless book every completion is correct. Whatever they supply becomes the official text of this read.

cards.prompt_text: She puts on her...
cards.follow_up: Getting-dressed pages are perfect: shoes, hat, coat. Point at the item while you pause.

cards.prompt_text: What happened to the boat?
cards.follow_up: Flip back to check together. Checking is not cheating; it's how recall gets built.

cards.prompt_text: Which animal came to the pond first?
cards.follow_up: Order words are the hidden curriculum here: first, next, last. Use them in your expansion.

cards.prompt_text: Before we turn the page, what has happened in the story so far?
cards.follow_up: A mid-book recap is retelling practice. Prompt with 'and then what?' as many times as they'll take.

cards.prompt_text: At the start, why didn't the bear want to sleep?
cards.follow_up: Why-recall is harder than what-recall. Any reasonable theory is a good answer; the book's answer is just one option.

cards.prompt_text: What was hiding under there?
cards.follow_up: Ask right after closing the flap, then open it again to check. Peekaboo memory is still recall.

cards.prompt_text: Where did the tractor go after the barn?
cards.follow_up: If they shrug, offer two choices: 'The field, or the pond?' Choices scaffold recall without giving it away.

cards.prompt_text: What happened when the milk spilled?
cards.follow_up: Cause-and-effect recall. Expand with feeling words: 'Right, she was frustrated, and then she got a towel.'

cards.prompt_text: At the end of the book: what was your favorite thing that happened?
cards.follow_up: Favorite-part recall is the gentlest retelling prompt there is, and it tells you what to talk about next.

cards.prompt_text: Tell me about this page.
cards.follow_up: Then be quiet longer than feels polite. Whatever arrives, add exactly one detail and hand it back.

cards.prompt_text: What's happening in this picture?
cards.follow_up: Point at the busiest part of the page. Accept fragments; your expansion turns fragments into sentences.

cards.prompt_text: What do you think happens next?
cards.follow_up: Prediction is open-ended plus suspense. Turn the page to test the theory, and honor near-misses loudly.

cards.prompt_text: Point to the page and ask: what do you see?
cards.follow_up: One word is a full answer at this age. 'Dog!' becomes 'Yes! A big brown dog.'

cards.prompt_text: Tell me the story of this page in your own words.
cards.follow_up: Let them narrate; you turn pages on their command. Being the reader is the point.

cards.prompt_text: What's going on here, and how do you know?
cards.follow_up: The 'how do you know' half builds evidence-talk: 'Because he's crying' is picture-reading, which is real reading.

cards.prompt_text: Tell me about this truck.
cards.follow_up: Expect parts-naming: wheels, lights, ladder. Expand with function: 'Yes, the ladder, for reaching high windows.'

cards.prompt_text: Where is the duck?
cards.follow_up: Pointing is a complete answer. Name what they found: 'There's the duck, behind the log!'

cards.prompt_text: What is that called?
cards.follow_up: Point at one clear thing. If no answer comes, name it warmly and move on; the question still taught the word.

cards.prompt_text: Who is eating the banana?
cards.follow_up: Who-questions attach people to actions. Expand with the verb: 'Yes, the monkey is eating it all up.'

cards.prompt_text: What is she doing?
cards.follow_up: Verb-hunting. Accept the noun answer and supply the verb: 'Right, the girl. She's climbing.'

cards.prompt_text: Where does the moon go in this picture?
cards.follow_up: Position words are the prize: up, behind, over. Use one in your expansion.

cards.prompt_text: Why do you think he is sad?
cards.follow_up: Why-questions about feelings are theory-of-mind practice. Every theory is admissible evidence.

cards.prompt_text: What are the wheels doing in the mud?
cards.follow_up: Odd questions get better answers than obvious ones. Expect 'spinning!' and expand from there.

cards.prompt_text: How is the boy going to fix it?
cards.follow_up: How-questions invite plans. Compare their plan with the book's on the next page.

cards.prompt_text: Who is under the flap?
cards.follow_up: Ask before lifting, guess together, then check. Wrong guesses are the fun part.

cards.prompt_text: Have you ever eaten a berry like that one?
cards.follow_up: Any memory counts, real or aspirational. Follow their thread away from the book; that's success, not derailment.

cards.prompt_text: That dog is muddy, like when we saw the dog at the park.
cards.follow_up: A statement works as well as a question. Pause after it; toddlers answer statements too.

cards.prompt_text: The bear brushes his teeth, just like you do at your house.
cards.follow_up: Then ask what comes next in THEIR bedtime. Comparing routines is sequencing practice in disguise.

cards.prompt_text: Have you ever felt as mad as she looks right there?
cards.follow_up: Feeling bridges are the deepest distancing prompts. Share one of your own mad moments back; reciprocity keeps it safe.

cards.prompt_text: We saw a digger like that when we walked to the store.
cards.follow_up: If the memory lands, ask what the real one was doing. Book paused, conversation running: exactly right.

cards.prompt_text: What would you do if your tower fell like his did?
cards.follow_up: Hypotheticals about their own life mix distancing with planning. Accept revenge-on-the-blocks answers gracefully.

cards.prompt_text: Who does this grandma remind you of in your own family?
cards.follow_up: Family bridges give the biggest payoff per question. Expect a story; abandon the book for it happily.

cards.prompt_text: That looks like the rain boots you wear, doesn't it?
cards.follow_up: Object bridges are the easiest distancing on-ramp for younger readers. One point at the page, one point at the shoe rack.
